summary:
Balıkesir is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework, in which hostility toward trans people operates as organised state policy rather than residual prejudice. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, about two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A draft omnibus law, the 11th Judicial Package, was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, penalise participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on condition of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. Its pending status has not stopped authorities from applying equivalent prohibitions in practice.

Street-level enforcement is documented. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district, in streets, shops and cafés, and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue these checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as it was already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk wherever appearance does not match the passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required electronic reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. No incident specific to Balıkesir appears in the sources; the province is governed by the national measures described here.
tangentialFactors:
The draft package's status is unsettled: Human Rights Watch reported it as pending in October 2025, and the woman detained in Istanbul stated that the law had not yet been passed while enforcement was already being applied to her. Enforcement running ahead of legislation is the operative pattern for a visitor, not the legislative timetable.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the depth of the regime rather than as a statement of current law.

Kaos GL's 2025 findings, presented at a report launch, describe anti-LGBTI+ hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy: hate speech by senior officials, instructions issued to public institutions under a Year of the Family banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Human Rights Watch separately identifies protecting the family and public morals as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.

Scale is national and rising: 313 recorded violations in 2025 against roughly 125 implied by the two-and-a-half-fold comparison with 2024, and 299 detention decisions of which 43 were not recorded through formal channels.
localsOnly:
Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated demands for an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Residents face the draft package's provisions directly: criminalisation of conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, up to four years' imprisonment for taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, a rise in the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 conditioned on permanent infertility, and punishment of health professionals who perform such care. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, issued after the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular added gender reassignment as an official medical-board reason, removes the other option from hospital records and mandates electronic reports, which risks profiling trans patients and restricting transition care. Online framing of the change as an LGBT opening has been contested.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory describes an incident, enforcement action or facility specific to Balıkesir. The province-level assessment rests entirely on national measures and on incidents documented in Istanbul, Ankara and Kayseri; whether provincial police in Balıkesir conduct comparable identity checks is not sourced.

The 11th Judicial Package was reported as a draft in October 2025. Whether it has since been adopted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the sources and cannot be stated either way.

The claim that GBT checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts cited in reporting; no court ruling on the point appears in the inventory.

The classification of three 2025 deaths as hate killings is the assessment of rights organisations, and the tally of six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence is not broken down by province or by legal outcome.

The Human Rights Watch 2008 material is historical and predates post-2018 legal changes; it should not be read as a statement of current law.
